t: 3605. Minimum Stability Factor of Array — Editorial
o:
## Understanding the problem
A subarray is stable if its HCF ≥ 2 (single elements ≥ 2 count). You may overwrite up to maxC elements with any integers; minimize the longest stable subarray remaining. Example 3: [2,4,9,6] has two disjoint stable blocks, so one change cannot destroy both — answer 2.

Monotonicity holds: if we can cap stability at L, we can cap it at any larger L. So binary search on the answer L, and for each L check feasibility: every window of length L+1 with gcd ≥ 2 must contain at least one modified element. This is interval stabbing — greedily change the rightmost element of the leftmost violating window, which covers the maximum number of future windows.
k: Feasibility is monotone in L, enabling binary search on the answer.
Each modification can be imagined as setting an element to 1, killing every stable window containing it — a hitting-set problem solvable greedily.
Range-gcd queries via a sparse table make each feasibility check O(n).

a.n: Approach 1: Binary search + greedy window stabbing
a.i: check(L): scan windows of length L+1 left to right with a sparse-table gcd. When a window has gcd ≥ 2, spend one change at its rightmost endpoint and jump the scan past that index (every window starting inside the previous one contains it, and the change makes its gcd 1). Feasible iff changes used ≤ maxC. Binary search the smallest feasible L.
s: Build a sparse table for O(1) range gcd.
Binary search L in [0, n]; for each mid run check(mid).
check: i = 0; while i + L < n: if gcd(i, i+L) ≥ 2, cnt++, i = i+L+1 else i++. Return cnt ≤ maxC.
a.t: O(n log n · log n) — sparse table build O(n log n), log n binary-search steps each running an O(n) check with O(1) gcd queries.
a.sp: O(n log n) for the sparse table.

w: Present binary search + greedy as the main solution. Pitfalls: after a change you must skip the scan to i+L+1 (windows overlapping the changed index are automatically safe), and remember L can be 0 when maxC covers every element ≥ 2. Follow-up: what if modifications must set elements to specific values, or queries ask for stability of ranges?
